claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Previous, prolonged or repeated exposures to a noxious stimulus can shift the nociceptive threshold up or down.
claims.source: The presence of other type of stress (Amit and Galina, 1986), as well as previous, prolonged or repeated exposures to a noxious stimulus (Schild et al., 2014), is able to shift the threshold up, inducing a desensitization, or down, inducing a sensitization.
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The development of chronic pain in humans can be related to maladaptive sensory plasticity.
claims.source: In humans, the development of some health problems, like chronic pain, can be related to maladaptive sensory plasticity (Pace et al., 2006; Gold and Gebhart, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: C. elegans is a powerful and tractable genetic model that exhibits considerable sensory plasticity.
claims.source: As a complementary model, the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans is a powerful and tractable genetic model, which exhibits considerable sensory plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism.

claims.claim: C. elegans can remember many types of environmental stimuli and display remarkable associative learning capabilities.
claims.source: Worms are able to remember many types of environmental stimuli and display remarkable associative learning capabilities (Ardiel and Rankin, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: C. elegans avoidance behaviors constitute useful paradigms to study nociceptive plasticity.
claims.source: Avoidance behaviors, which C. elegans executes in response to noxious stimuli, constitute useful paradigms to study nociceptive plasticity (Schild et al., 2014; de Bono and Maricq, 2005; Meisel and Kim, 2014; Komuniecki et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: C. elegans engages multiple thermosensory behaviors to stay away or escape from noxious heat above 26°C.
claims.source: C. elegans engages multiple thermosensory behaviors in order to stay away or escape from noxious heat, when placed in different regions of a spatial thermogradient reaching harmful temperatures (>26°C for the worm) (Schild and Glauser, 2013; Glauser, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: When acutely stimulated with heat, C. elegans produces a robust, stereotyped thermal avoidance behavior consisting of reversal and reorientation.
claims.source: When acutely stimulated with heat, worms produce a robust, stereotyped thermal avoidance behavior, consisting in a worm reversal with a short backward movement, followed by a reorientation maneuver (Wittenburg and Baumeister, 1999; Ghosh et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The thermal withdrawal behavior relies on two pairs of head primary thermosensory neurons named AFDs and FLPs.
claims.source: This withdrawal behavior relies on two pairs of head primary thermosensory neurons named AFDs and FLPs (Liu et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: AFD neuron plays a major role in controlling thermotaxis in the innocuous temperature range.
claims.source: AFD neuron also plays a major role in controlling thermotaxis in the innocuous temperature range, being both an exquisitely sensitive thermal detector and an essential memory and plasticity locus (Goodman and Sengupta, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: AFD can detect tiny changes in temperature.
claims.source: Indeed, AFD can detect tiny changes in temperature (Ramot et al., 2008b) and produce intracellular calcium transients in response to temperature elevations above a certain threshold, which depends on past thermosensory experience and which is determined by cell-autonomous mechanisms (Kobayashi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: AFD produces intracellular calcium transients in response to temperature elevations above a threshold that depends on past thermosensory experience.
claims.source: Indeed, AFD can detect tiny changes in temperature (Ramot et al., 2008b) and produce intracellular calcium transients in response to temperature elevations above a certain threshold, which depends on past thermosensory experience and which is determined by cell-autonomous mechanisms (Kobayashi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The AFD thermal response threshold is determined by cell-autonomous mechanisms.
claims.source: Indeed, AFD can detect tiny changes in temperature (Ramot et al., 2008b) and produce intracellular calcium transients in response to temperature elevations above a certain threshold, which depends on past thermosensory experience and which is determined by cell-autonomous mechanisms (Kobayashi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: FLP neurons are thermosensors responding over a broad thermal range from 8 to 38°C with steeper sensitivity in the noxious heat range.
claims.source: FLP neurons are thermosensors responding over a broad thermal range, from 8 to 38°C, with a steeper sensitivity in the noxious heat range (Saro et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Temperature is encoded in FLP via a tonic signaling mode with activity level and steady-state intracellular calcium concentration reflecting the currently experienced temperature.
claims.source: Temperature is encoded in FLP via a tonic signaling mode, with the activity level and steady-state intracellular calcium concentration reflecting the currently experienced temperature (Saro et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The primary FLP thermosensory response to short-lasting heat stimuli is largely nonadaptable and unaffected by past thermal history.
claims.source: The primary FLP thermosensory response to short-lasting heat stimuli seems largely nonadaptable, remaining unaffected by past thermal history.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on previous knowledge.

claims.claim: FLP outputs can be modulated and take part in experience-dependent plasticity of the nociceptive response.
claims.source: However, many lines of evidence indicate that FLP outputs can be modulated (Schild et al., 2014; Saro et al., 2020), taking part in the experience-dependent plasticity of the nociceptive response.
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Upon prolonged or repeated exposure to noxious heat, worms increase their thermal threshold for heat responsiveness through a desensitization, analgesia-like effect.
claims.source: Indeed, upon prolonged or repeated exposure to noxious heat, worms increase their thermal threshold for heat responsiveness through a desensitization, analgesia-like effect (Schild et al., 2014; Lia and Glauser, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In both AFD and FLP, experience-dependent plasticity involves the cell-autonomous activity of CMK-1.
claims.source: In both AFD and FLP, as well as additional sensory neurons, experience-dependent plasticity involves the cell-autonomous activity of the calcium/calmodulin (CaM)-dependent protein kinase-1 (CMK-1) (Schild et al., 2014; Satterlee et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2014; Neal et al., 2015; Moss et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: CMK-1 is a Ser/Thr protein kinase widely expressed throughout the nervous system.
claims.source: CMK-1 is a Ser/Thr protein kinase widely expressed throughout the nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CMK-1.

claims.claim: Mammalian CaMKI and CaMKIV function as intracellular Ca2+ signaling effectors in the nervous system.
claims.source: It is the only homologue of the mammalian CaM kinases I and IV (CaMKI and CaMKIV) both functioning as intracellular Ca2+ signaling effector in the nervous system (Soderling, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: CaM kinases play a role in gene transcription, signal transduction, synaptic development and plasticity, memory and experience-dependent behaviors.
claims.source: CaM kinases play a role in processes including gene transcription, signal transduction, synaptic development and plasticity, memory and experience-dependent behaviors (Satterlee et al., 2004; Hook and Means, 2001; Wayman et al., 2008b; Dahiya et al., 2019; Ardiel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: CMK-1 signaling pathway is functionally conserved from nematodes to humans.
claims.source: CMK-1 signaling pathway is functionally conserved from nematodes to humans (Eto et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: CMK-1 protein topology comprises an extended N-terminal kinase catalytic domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain.
claims.source: CMK-1 protein topology is also well-conserved. It comprises an extended N-terminal kinase catalytic domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain, which includes an autoinhibitory domain that partially overlaps with a CaM binding domain (Hook and Means, 2001; Goldberg et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The CMK-1 regulatory domain includes an autoinhibitory domain that partially overlaps with a CaM binding domain.
claims.source: It comprises an extended N-terminal kinase catalytic domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain, which includes an autoinhibitory domain that partially overlaps with a CaM binding domain (Hook and Means, 2001; Goldberg et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the absence of Ca2+/CaM binding, the CMK-1 regulatory domain maintains the catalytic domain in an inactive state.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+/CaM binding, the regulatory domain maintains the catalytic domain in an inactive state.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CaM kinase regulation.

claims.claim: The binding of Ca2+/CaM causes a conformational change in CMK-1 that releases the autoinhibition.
claims.source: The binding of Ca2+/CaM causes a conformational change in the protein that releases the autoinhibition.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CaM kinase regulation.

claims.claim: The subcellular localization of CaM kinases is subject to dynamic regulation.
claims.source: The subcellular localization of CaM kinases is subject to dynamic regulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: The nuclear localization of δCaMKI, γCaMKI, and some CaMKII isoforms depends on the cell-activation state.
claims.source: Hence, the nuclear localization of δCaMKI, γCaMKI, and some CaMKII isoforms depends on the cell-activation state (Sakagami et al., 2005; Cohen et al., 2016; Schulman, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The mechanisms causing cell-activation dependent translocation of CaMKII are well-characterized.
claims.source: Whereas the mechanisms causing the translocation of CaMKII in a cell-activation dependent manner are well-characterized (Zalcman et al., 2018), those controlling CaMKI nuclear translocation and their physiological relevance in vivo are less well understood.
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The mechanisms controlling CaMKI nuclear translocation and their physiological relevance in vivo are less well understood.
claims.source: Whereas the mechanisms causing the translocation of CaMKII in a cell-activation dependent manner are well-characterized (Zalcman et al., 2018), those controlling CaMKI nuclear translocation and their physiological relevance in vivo are less well understood.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claims.claim: At innocuous temperatures, CMK-1 is localized principally in the cytoplasm of FLP where it contributes to maintain a low behavioral response threshold to promote heat avoidance.
claims.source: In FLP, CMK-1 plays a dual role in the heat-avoidance behavior. At innocuous temperatures, CMK-1 is localized principally in the cytoplasm, where it contributes to maintain a low behavioral response threshold to promote heat avoidance.
claims.evidence: This is stated and based on previous work cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Within 1 hr of acclimation at 28°C, CMK-1 progressively translocates into the nucleus of FLP where it raises the noxious heat threshold to reduce avoidance.
claims.source: Within 1 hr of acclimation at 28°C (moderately noxious temperature), CMK-1 progressively translocates into the nucleus, where it produces the opposite effect, raising the noxious heat threshold to reduce avoidance (Schild et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In AFD, CMK-1 changes its subcellular localization upon temperature shifts during which cultivation temperature memory is reset.
claims.source: In AFD, CMK-1 also changes its subcellular localization upon temperature shifts, during which cultivation temperature memory is reset (Yu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The subcellular redistribution of CMK-1 appears to have a major role in adjusting neuron outputs according to past sensory experience.
claims.source: The subcellular redistribution of CMK-1 thus appears to have a major role in adjusting neuron outputs according to past sensory experience.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the described observations.

claims.claim: The molecular mechanisms through which sensory experience controls CMK-1 subcellular localization are largely unknown.
claims.source: However, the molecular mechanisms through which sensory experience controls CMK-1 subcellular localization are largely unknown.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claims.claim: In naïve animals grown at 20°C, CMK-1 is mostly localized in the cytoplasm of FLP.
claims.source: In naïve animals (grown at 20°C), CMK-1 is mostly localized in the cytoplasm of FLP (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Exposure to 28°C causes CMK-1 to progressively translocate into the nucleus of FLP, being slightly enriched in the nucleus after 90 min.
claims.source: Exposure to moderately noxious temperature (28°C) causes CMK-1 to progressively translocate into the nucleus, being slightly enriched in the nucleus after 90 min (Figure 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: Disrupting the NES288-294 candidate sequence with V292A/V294A double mutation or Δ288–294 deletion prevented the cytoplasmic expression of CMK-1 and yielded nuclear accumulation.
claims.source: Disrupting the NES288-294 candidate sequence with a V292A/V294A double mutation or a Δ288–294 deletion prevented the cytoplasmic expression of CMK-1 and even yielded a nuclear accumulation (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: NES315-323 candidate mutants displayed a cytoplasmic enrichment similar to that of wild-type CMK-1.
claims.source: In contrast, NES315-323 candidate mutants displayed a cytoplasmic enrichment similar to that of wild-type CMK-1. These included I315A single mutant, V321A/V323A double mutant, I315A/V321A/V323A triple mutant, as well as Δ318–324 and Δ315–323 mutants, in which the NES candidate region is deleted in part or in full (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: NES288-294 is a key determinant of CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization in FLP at 20°C.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that the NES288-294, but not the NES314-323, is a key determinant of CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization in FLP at 20°C.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutational analysis data.

claims.claim: Inhibiting exportins with leptomycin B caused CMK-1::mNG nuclear translocation in FLP neurons at 20°C.
claims.source: Inhibiting exportins with the leptomycin B pharmacological inhibitor (Kudo et al., 1999) caused CMK-1::mNG nuclear translocation in FLP neurons at 20°C (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The predominant cytoplasmic expression of CMK-1 at 20°C in FLP requires NES288-294 and relies on an exportin-dependent active nuclear export mechanism.
claims.source: Collectively, these results suggest that the predominant cytoplasmic expression of CMK-1 at 20°C in FLP requires NES288-294 and relies on an exportin-dependent active nuclear export mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the NES mutation and leptomycin B data.

claims.claim: Mutations affecting the NLS71-78 candidate region significantly impaired the nuclear relocalization of CMK-1 after prolonged heat exposure.
claims.source: Mutations affecting the NLS71-78 candidate region all significantly impaired the nuclear relocalization of CMK-1 after prolonged heat exposure (Figure 1F, right).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of NLS71-78 mutations on CMK-1 nuclear relocalization was partial in CMK-1(K71A) and CMK-1(R74Q) single mutants and complete in the CMK-1(R77S) single mutant and CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S) triple mutant.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect was partial in CMK-1(K71A) and CMK-1(R74Q) single mutants and complete in the CMK-1(R77S) single mutant, as well as in the CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S) triple mutant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text describing the results shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Mutations in the NLS297-307 candidate region produced a partial reduction in CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
claims.source: Introducing mutations in the NLS297-307 candidate region (K307Q single mutant or a R302S/K307Q double mutant) also produced a partial reduction in CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text describing the results shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: NLS-affecting mutations did not modulate the baseline cytoplasmic expression of CMK-1 at 20°C.
claims.source: In contrast, none of the NLS-affecting mutations modulated the baseline cytoplasmic expression at 20°C (Figure 1F, left), suggesting that these elements might not be active in the absence of prolonged cell stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: NLS71-78 and NLS297-308 are only engaged upon prolonged thermal stimulation.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest that (i) the canonical importin pathway may be involved, (ii) NLS71-78 and NLS297-308 are only engaged upon prolonged thermal stimulation, and (iii) NLS71-78 plays a major role and NLS297-308 a more minor role in driving CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the NLS mutation data.

claims.claim: NLS71-78 plays a major role and NLS297-308 a more minor role in driving CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest that (i) the canonical importin pathway may be involved, (ii) NLS71-78 and NLS297-308 are only engaged upon prolonged thermal stimulation, and (iii) NLS71-78 plays a major role and NLS297-308 a more minor role in driving CMK-1 nuclear accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the NLS mutation data.

claims.claim: A prolonged heat treatment can cause CMK-1 nuclear relocalization in unc-13 mutants with impaired synaptic transmission.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, we found that a prolonged heat treatment could still cause CMK-1 nuclear relocalization in unc-13 mutants with impaired synaptic transmission (Richmond et al., 1999) and in unc-31 mutants with impaired neuropeptide signaling (Speese et al., 2007; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A prolonged heat treatment can cause CMK-1 nuclear relocalization in unc-31 mutants with impaired neuropeptide signaling.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, we found that a prolonged heat treatment could still cause CMK-1 nuclear relocalization in unc-13 mutants with impaired synaptic transmission (Richmond et al., 1999) and in unc-31 mutants with impaired neuropeptide signaling (Speese et al., 2007; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The mechanisms leading to temperature-dependent CMK-1 nuclear relocalization could primarily depend on cell-autonomous heat-evoked FLP activity.
claims.source: These results suggest that the mechanisms leading to temperature-dependent CMK-1 nuclear relocalization could primarily depend on cell-autonomous heat-evoked FLP activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the unc-13 and unc-31 mutant data.

claims.claim: In unc-68(dom13) mutants, CMK-1 nuclear expression was stronger at 20°C compared to wild-type.
claims.source: In comparison to wild-type, CMK-1 nuclear expression was stronger at 20°C in unc-68(dom13) mutants (Figure 2B, top).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: A chronic elevation in intracellular Ca2+ levels in unc-68(dom13) mutants is sufficient to favor CMK-1 accumulation in the nucleus.
claims.source: These data suggest that a chronic elevation in intracellular Ca2+ levels in the unc-68(dom13) mutants is sufficient to favor CMK-1 accumulation in the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the unc-68(dom13) data.

claims.claim: Calbindin overexpression in FLP significantly impaired CMK-1 accumulation in the nucleus at 28°C.
claims.source: Then, we evaluated CMK-1 localization and found that, whereas the localization of CMK-1 at 20°C was indistinguishable from that in wild-type, Calbindin overexpression in FLP significantly impaired its accumulation in the nucleus at 28°C (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Parvalbumin significantly reduced the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1 at 28°C.
claims.source: Overexpressing another Ca2+ buffer, Parvalbumin, also significantly reduced the nuclear accumulation of CMK-1 at 28°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: A mutant Parvalbumin with mutations affecting all its calcium binding sites did not impair CMK-1 localization.
claims.source: In contrast, a mutant Parvalbumin with mutations affecting all its calcium binding sites did not impair CMK-1 localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that the effect of Parvalbumin involves its Ca2+ binding activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: An elevation of intracellular Ca2+ in FLP is required for CMK-1 nuclear translocation upon prolonged thermal stimulation.
claims.source: Collectively, the results of Ca2+ buffering experiments suggest that an elevation of intracellular Ca2+ in FLP is required for CMK-1 nuclear translocation upon prolonged thermal stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the calcium buffering experiments.

claims.claim: Mutations in genes coding for L- and N-type voltage-gated calcium channels, TRP channels, and ryanodine receptor did not cause significant alteration of CMK-1 localization.
claims.source: In an attempt to identify specific Ca2+-permeable channels involved, we evaluated the impact of reduction-of-function mutations in the genes coding for the L- and N-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC; egl-19(n582), unc-2(gk355), unc-2(ra612)), for transient receptor potential channels (ocr-2(ak47); osm-9(ky5) double mutants) and for the ryanodine receptor (unc-68(r1161)). These mutations had previously been shown to affect FLP Ca2+ response to short stimuli lasting between 30 s and 5 min (Saro et al., 2020). Contrary to our expectations, none of these mutations caused a significant alteration of CMK-1 localization (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: None of the calcium channel mutations significantly affected the Ca2+ elevation caused by a 60 min incubation at 28°C.
claims.source: Interestingly, none of the mutations significantly affected the Ca2+elevation caused by a 60 min incubation at 28°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The CMK-1(W305S) mutation prevented CMK-1 nuclear translocation into the nucleus upon prolonged heat stimulation at 28°C.
claims.source: This CMK-1 mutation had a similar effect to the buffering of calcium with exogenous Ca2+buffers, preventing CMK-1 nuclear translocation into the nucleus upon prolonged heat stimulation (28°C, Figure 2B, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The W305S mutation was able to counteract the CMK-1 nuclear accumulation observed in unc-68(dom13) mutant with permanently elevated calcium levels.
claims.source: Furthermore, the W305S mutation was also able to counteract the CMK-1 nuclear accumulation observed in unc-68(dom13) mutant with permanently elevated calcium levels (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Prolonged thermal stimulation causes prolonged cell-autonomous FLP thermosensory activity, long-lasting changes in intracellular calcium concentration and binding of Ca2+/CaM on CMK-1 to promote CMK-1 nuclear translocation.
claims.source: Collectively, these results are consistent with a model in which prolonged thermal stimulation causes prolonged cell-autonomous FLP thermosensory activity, long-lasting changes in intracellular calcium concentration and binding of Ca2+/CaM on CMK-1 to promote CMK-1 nuclear translocation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the calcium manipulation and W305S mutation data.

claims.claim: CMK-1(V292A/V294A/W305S) triple mutant protein expression was cytoplasmic at 28°C, indistinguishable from that of the single W305S mutant.
claims.source: Contrary to the predication made according to the NES masking model, we found that the triple mutant protein expression was cytoplasmic at 28°C, indistinguishable from that of the single W305S mutant (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A functional NES288-294 element is dispensable for the cytosolic retention at 28°C of CaM binding-disruption mutant CMK-1.
claims.source: Therefore, a functional NES288-294 element is dispensable for the cytosolic retention at 28°C of CaM binding-disruption mutant CMK-1.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the triple mutant data.

claims.claim: The masking of the NES288-294 element upon CaM binding to CMK-1(wt) is unlikely to be a major mechanism promoting CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C.
claims.source: These data suggest that the masking of the NES288-294 element upon CaM binding to CMK-1(wt) is unlikely to be a major mechanism promoting CMK-1 nuclear accumulation at 28°C.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the triple mutant data.

claims.claim: The expression of the NLS71-78 mutant CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S) was significantly more cytoplasmic than CMK-1(wt) in the unc-68(dom13) high-calcium background at both 20 and 28°C.
claims.source: This was indeed the case as the expression of the NLS71-78 mutant CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S) was significantly more cytoplasmic than CMK-1(wt) in the unc-68(dom13), high-calcium background at both 20 and 28°C (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S/V292A/V294) mutant protein was excluded from the cytoplasm similarly to CMK-1(V292A/V294) mutant protein at 20°C.
claims.source: We therefore evaluated the localization of a CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S/V292A/V294) mutant combining NLS71-78- and NES288-294-disrupting mutations (Figure 3E). According to our prediction, this mutant protein was excluded from the cytoplasm similarly to CMK-1(V292A/V294) mutant protein lacking only the functional NES288-294 element.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: At 20°C, when calcium levels are low and there is little CaM binding to CMK-1, the NLS71-78 element is not engaged to regulate CMK-1 localization.
claims.source: Therefore, at 20°C, when calcium levels are low and there is little CaM binding to CMK-1, the NLS71-78 element is not engaged to regulate CMK-1 localization.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined NLS/NES mutant data.

claims.claim: IMA-3 is the only importin-α isoform expressed in somatic tissues in C. elegans.
claims.source: Three importin-α are encoded in the C. elegans genome (IMA-1, -2, and -3). Previous data suggest that IMA-3 is the only isoform expressed in somatic tissues (Geles and Adam, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: ima-3 is expressed in FLP neurons.
claims.source: We confirmed the broad somatic expression of ima-3 using an [ima-3p::NLS::wrmScarlet] reporter. Expressing cells included FLP neurons, as judged with the green/red co-labeling with the mec-3p::CMK-1::mNG reporter (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In the absence of Ca2+/CaM, CMK-1 had a relatively low but detectable affinity for IMA-3 with Kd ≈ 1.54 μM.
claims.source: In the absence of Ca2+/CaM, CMK-1 had a relatively low but detectable affinity for IMA-3 (Kd ≈ 1.54 μM).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: In the presence of Ca2+/CaM (2 mM Ca2+ and 8 µM CaM), the affinity of CMK-1 for IMA-3 raised by about approximately threefold to Kd ≈ 0.45 μM.
claims.source: In the presence of Ca2+/CaM (2 mM Ca2+ and 8 µM CaM), the affinity for IMA-3 raised by about approximately threefold (Kd ≈ 0.45 μM).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1 and Figure 4B.

claims.claim: No significant increase in CMK-1/IMA-3 affinity was seen with Ca2+ only (2 mM Ca2+, no CaM).
claims.source: No significant increase in affinity was seen with Ca2+ only (2 mM Ca2+, no CaM).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: The binding of Ca2+/CaM to CMK-1 is sufficient to increase its affinity to IMA-3.
claims.source: These data suggest that the binding of Ca2+/CaM to CMK-1 is sufficient to increase its affinity to IMA-3.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MST data.

claims.claim: The NLS71-78 of CMK-1 mediates a major part of the Ca2+/CaM-binding-dependent IMA-3 affinity increase.
claims.source: This increased affinity effect was significantly reduced in CMK-1(K71A/R74Q/R77S) triple mutant, furthermore suggesting that the NLS71-78 of CMK-1 mediates a major part of the Ca2+/CaM-binding-dependent IMA-3 affinity increase.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claims.claim: Loss of cmk-1 in cmk-1(ok287) mutants increased animal responsiveness to acute heat stimuli.
claims.source: Similar to previous findings (Lia and Glauser, 2020), loss of cmk-1 in cmk-1(ok287) mutants increased the animal responsiveness to acute stimuli (Figure 5B).

results.result: NES288-294 is a functional nuclear export sequence that maintains CMK-1 cytoplasmic localization in FLP neurons at 20°C through exportin-dependent active transport. Mutations disrupting NES288-294 (V292A/V294A or Δ288-294) cause nuclear accumulation, while mutations in the alternative NES315-323 candidate have no effect. Leptomycin B treatment also causes nuclear translocation, confirming exportin dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 provide converging evidence from mutational analysis (C51-C52), pharmacological inhibition (C54), and localization data (C49-C50) that collectively demonstrate NES288-294 is the functional nuclear export sequence. The negative results with NES315-323 mutants strengthen the conclusion by ruling out alternative sequences.

results.result: NLS71-78 is the major nuclear localization signal required for CMK-1 nuclear translocation upon prolonged heat exposure (28°C, 90 min), with NLS297-308 playing a minor role. These NLS elements are only engaged during prolonged thermal stimulation and do not affect baseline cytoplasmic localization at 20°C.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 demonstrate through systematic mutational analysis that NLS71-78 mutations completely block (R77S) or partially impair (K71A, R74Q) nuclear translocation at 28°C, while having no effect at 20°C. The temperature-dependent engagement and differential roles of the two NLS elements are well-supported by the data in Figure 1F.

results.result: Temperature-dependent CMK-1 nuclear relocalization in FLP neurons is cell-autonomous and does not require synaptic transmission or neuropeptide signaling. CMK-1 nuclear translocation occurs normally in unc-13 and unc-31 mutants with impaired neurotransmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by data in Figure 2A showing that mutations affecting synaptic transmission (unc-13) and neuropeptide signaling (unc-31) do not prevent heat-induced CMK-1 nuclear translocation. However, the authors acknowledge they cannot rule out redundant functions or electrical synapses, which introduces minor uncertainty.

results.result: Elevated intracellular Ca2+ is both necessary and sufficient for CMK-1 nuclear translocation in FLP neurons. The unc-68(dom13) gain-of-function mutation with chronically elevated Ca2+ causes nuclear accumulation at 20°C, while Ca2+ buffering with Calbindin or Parvalbumin prevents nuclear translocation at 28°C in a Ca2+-binding-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 provide bidirectional evidence: gain-of-function (C65-C66) and loss-of-function (C67-C69) manipulations of Ca2+ levels produce the predicted effects on CMK-1 localization. The control with mutant Parvalbumin (C69) strengthens the conclusion that Ca2+ binding activity is required. The data in Figures 2B-C and supplements support these claims.

results.result: Individual mutations in L-type and N-type voltage-gated calcium channels, TRP channels, or ryanodine receptor do not significantly affect CMK-1 localization or the Ca2+ elevation caused by 60 min incubation at 28°C, suggesting redundancy or involvement of other channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 report negative results that are well-documented in Figure 2D and supplement 2B. The authors appropriately interpret these findings as suggesting either redundancy among channels or involvement of unidentified channels. The negative results are important for understanding the mechanism but do not identify the specific Ca2+ sources.

results.result: Ca2+/CaM binding to CMK-1 is required for nuclear translocation. The W305S mutation, which disrupts CaM binding, prevents CMK-1 nuclear translocation at 28°C and counteracts the nuclear accumulation in unc-68(dom13) mutants with elevated Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 demonstrate through the W305S mutation that CaM binding is essential for Ca2+-dependent nuclear translocation. The mutation blocks translocation both in wild-type at 28°C and in the high-calcium unc-68(dom13) background (Figure 2B), providing strong evidence for the requirement of Ca2+/CaM binding.

results.result: The NES masking model is rejected: Ca2+/CaM binding does not promote nuclear accumulation by masking NES288-294. The triple mutant CMK-1(V292A/V294A/W305S) remains cytoplasmic at 28°C like the W305S single mutant, demonstrating that a functional NES is dispensable when CaM binding is disrupted.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 use a critical genetic test (Figure 3B) to rule out the NES masking mechanism. The logic is sound: if CaM binding masked the NES, then disrupting both should allow nuclear entry, but the triple mutant remains cytoplasmic. This negative result effectively eliminates one mechanistic hypothesis.

results.result: The NLS unmasking model is supported: NLS71-78 is only engaged when Ca2+ levels are elevated and CaM is bound to CMK-1. At 20°C with low Ca2+, NLS71-78 mutations have no effect even when NES288-294 is disrupted, but in the high-Ca2+ unc-68(dom13) background, NLS71-78 mutations significantly reduce nuclear accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 provide strong support for the NLS unmasking model through epistasis analysis (Figures 3D-E). The temperature- and calcium-dependent engagement of NLS71-78 is demonstrated by its differential effects in different genetic backgrounds, supporting the model that Ca2+/CaM binding exposes this NLS.

results.result: Ca2+/CaM binding to CMK-1 increases its affinity for IMA-3 importin approximately threefold (from Kd ≈ 1.54 μM to Kd ≈ 0.45 μM) in vitro. This increased affinity requires both Ca2+ and CaM, and is mediated primarily through NLS71-78, as the affinity increase is significantly reduced in the K71A/R74Q/R77S triple mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by quantitative MST binding data (Figure 4B-C, Table 1) showing the threefold affinity increase is statistically significant and depends on both Ca2+ and CaM. The NLS71-78 mutant analysis (C88) demonstrates this sequence mediates the affinity increase. The in vitro biochemical data directly support the proposed mechanism.

results.result: NES288-294 and NLS71-78 mutations have opposite effects on acute heat-evoked behavior: NES288-294 disruption (constitutive nuclear localization) reduces responsiveness, while NLS71-78 disruption has no effect. Loss of cmk-1 increases responsiveness, consistent with cytoplasmic CMK-1 promoting avoidance.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 5B showing differential effects of the mutations. The results are internally consistent with the localization data and the proposed dual roles of CMK-1 in different compartments. The cell-autonomous rescue experiments (C99) further support the FLP-specific function.

results.result: NLS71-78-dependent CMK-1 nuclear localization is essential for heat adaptation and desensitization. Wild-type animals show desensitization after 1 hr at 28°C (shifting toward higher temperatures in thermogradients), but this adaptation is impaired in cmk-1(ok287) null mutants and cmk-1(syb1435) R77S NLS mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 demonstrate the physiological importance of CMK-1 nuclear translocation using thermogradient assays (Figure 5C). The NLS mutant specifically impairs adaptation without affecting naive behavior, directly linking nuclear localization to the desensitization process. The data support the functional significance of the translocation mechanism.

results.result: NES288-294-controlled cytoplasmic retention of CMK-1 in FLP promotes reversal behavior by upregulating FLP outputs. Optogenetic activation of FLP produces fewer reversals in NES mutants with constitutive nuclear localization, while NLS mutants respond normally. Cell-specific rescue with the mec-3 promoter confirms FLP-autonomous function.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 use optogenetic analysis to isolate FLP-specific effects (Figure 5D-E). The cell-specific rescue (C99) is critical for demonstrating that the NES mutation acts within FLP rather than in downstream neurons. The data support the conclusion that cytoplasmic CMK-1 promotes FLP output.

results.result: Heat adaptation dampens FLP pathway responses downstream of thermal sensitivity, and this adaptation requires NLS71-78-dependent nuclear accumulation. Prolonged heat treatment (90 min at 28°C) reduces optogenetically-evoked reversals in wild-type but not in NLS71-78 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 demonstrate that adaptation occurs downstream of FLP thermosensation by using optogenetic stimulation (Figure 5F). The NLS mutant blocks this adaptation, directly linking nuclear CMK-1 to the dampening of pathway responses. This is a key result connecting molecular mechanism to behavioral plasticity.

results.result: CMK-1 localization in AFD neurons shows an opposite temperature dependence compared to FLP: CMK-1 is nuclear at 15°C and cytoplasmic at 25°C, the inverse of the pattern in FLP where high temperature promotes nuclear localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 are supported by clear localization data in Figures 6A-B showing opposite temperature effects in AFD versus FLP. This is a striking and important finding that demonstrates the mechanism can encode opposite signals in different neuron types, as stated in the abstract (C5).

results.result: Baseline intracellular calcium levels in AFD inversely correlate with growth temperature: animals grown at 15°C have significantly higher resting Ca2+ (YFP/CFP ratio = 1.09) than those at 25°C (ratio = 0.93), opposite to the pattern in FLP.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 and C128 report a novel finding about long-term calcium regulation in AFD using cameleon imaging (Figure 6D-E). The authors acknowledge this was previously unknown (C127) and provide quantitative data showing the inverse correlation. The magnitude of the difference (ΔR ≈ 0.16) is comparable to acute thermal responses, supporting its physiological significance.

results.result: The same Ca2+/CaM-dependent mechanism involving NLS71-78, NES288-294, and IMA-3 importin controls CMK-1 localization in both FLP and AFD neurons. Mutations in W305S (CaM binding), NLS71-78, and NES288-294 have similar effects on CMK-1 localization in AFD as in FLP.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C114 demonstrate the generality of the mechanism by showing that the same mutations affect CMK-1 localization in AFD (Figure 6B-C). The unc-68(dom13) experiments and ima-3 expression data (C113) further support that the same molecular machinery operates in both neuron types, despite opposite calcium responses to temperature.

results.result: Normal NES288-294- and NLS71-78-dependent CMK-1 localization control is essential for AFD function, including thermotaxis behavior and temperature-dependent gcy-8 gene expression. Both NLS and NES mutations abolish the growth-temperature effect on gcy-8 transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C120 demonstrate functional consequences of disrupted CMK-1 localization in AFD through thermotaxis assays (Figure 6G) and gcy-8 reporter analysis (Figure 6H-I). However, the interpretation is complicated: both NLS and NES mutations produce similar effects on gene expression despite having opposite effects on localization, suggesting dynamic shuttling rather than static localization may be important.

results.result: The proposed mechanism for CMK-1 localization control involves three key features: (1) functional NLS71-78 and NES288-294 sequences recognized by importins and exportins, (2) Ca2+/CaM binding that increases IMA-3 affinity threefold and unmasks NLS71-78, and (3) long-term modulation of steady-state Ca2+ levels producing slow redistribution kinetics (90 min) matching sensory adaptation timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 and C121-C125 synthesize the mechanistic model supported by the collective data. The three-part mechanism is well-supported by mutational analysis (NLS/NES), biochemical data (MST binding), calcium manipulation experiments, and kinetics measurements. The slow kinetics (C4) matching adaptation timescales is an important feature supported by Figure 1C.

results.result: The CMK-1 nuclear translocation mechanism enables encoding of opposite nuclear signals in neuron types with opposite calcium responses (FLP vs AFD) and is essential for experience-dependent behavioral plasticity and gene transcription control in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 represent the major conclusions of the paper, integrating findings from FLP and AFD. The opposite calcium responses (C106, C108) coupled with the same molecular mechanism produce opposite CMK-1 localization patterns. Behavioral (C93-C96, C101-C103) and transcriptional (C117-C119) data demonstrate in vivo functional importance.

results.result: The CMK-1 localization system filters out short-lasting calcium peaks to reflect global changes over longer timescales, controlling the intracellular locus of CaM kinase signaling on time frames longer than kinase autoinhibitory control. AFD calcium responses include both short-term responses to acute thermal change and a newly described resting calcium drift component with opposite temperature effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C126, C129-C130 present interpretive conclusions about the functional logic of the system. The slow kinetics (90 min) support the filtering hypothesis (C126), though this remains somewhat speculative. The dual timescale calcium responses in AFD (C129) are well-supported by the imaging data showing both acute responses and long-term baseline differences.

results.result: CMK-1 is the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian CaMKI/IV, which are conserved regulators of adaptable behaviors. Similar mechanisms may exist in other organisms and sensory modalities, particularly in tonically signaling sensory neurons subject to long-term calcium changes, due to the high conservation of Ca2+ signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C8 state established facts about CMK-1/CaMKI/IV conservation. Claims C9, C131-C132 are speculative extrapolations about potential conservation of the mechanism in other systems. While the speculation is reasonable given the conservation of the proteins and Ca2+ signaling, no direct evidence is provided for these mechanisms in other organisms or sensory modalities.
